why-react.name: What is React and why does it exist?
why-react.desc: Without React: updating the DOM manually is slow, tedious, and error-prone at scale. React solves this with a component model where you describe what the UI should look like, and React figures out how to update the DOM efficiently. Built by Facebook in 2013.
why-react.q: What problem does React solve? What was wrong with updating the DOM manually?
why-react.qsub: What is the difference between React the library and React DOM? Why are they separate packages?
why-react.what:
Definition: React is a JavaScript library for building UIs. Its core idea in one line — UI = f(state). You change the state, and React matches the screen to that state.

In vanilla JS you update the DOM by hand. In React you only change the data.
why-react.analogy: Ordering in a restaurant. Imperative = walking into the kitchen and saying "turn on the gas, add oil, chop the onions". Declarative = telling the waiter "one paneer tikka". How it’s made is the chef’s job.
why-react.why: As the app grows, manual DOM updates become exponentially difficult. One piece of data appears in five places — if it changes you must update all five, and missing one makes the UI and data diverge (this "state desync" bug is the most common). In React this is impossible because the UI is always derived from the state.
pros: State desync bugs are practically eliminated
Components are reusable — write once, use in 20 places
The largest ecosystem and job market
cons: It’s only a UI library — routing, data fetching have to be added separately
Bundle size is larger than vanilla
Overkill for a small static site
gotchas: React is not a framework, it’s a library — not everything is built-in like Angular
The Virtual DOM isn’t for being “fast”, it’s to make “declarative coding possible”
React builds UI from state — directly manipulating the DOM will confuse React

you specify step-by-step — grab this element, change this text, remove this class

setup.name: Setting up a React project — Vite, create-react-app, or Next.js
setup.desc: Vite: npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react → fastest setup. CRA: npx create-react-app my-app → older, slower. Next.js: npx create-next-app@latest → for SSR/full-stack. For learning React basics, use Vite.
setup.q: How do you create a new React project? What is the role of a bundler like Vite or Webpack?
setup.qsub: What does a bundler actually do? Why do you need it — why can't you just write React in a .html file?
setup.what:
Definition: There are three ways to start a React project — Vite (fast, simple SPA), Next.js (routing + SSR + backend all included), and CRA (create-react-app — now deprecated, don’t use it).

In 2026: use Vite for learning and SPAs. Use Next.js for production websites/products.

props-state-intro.name: Props vs State — passing data and managing change
props-state-intro.desc: Props: data passed FROM parent TO child — read-only, like function parameters. State: data that lives INSIDE a component — when it changes, React re-renders the component. Props are for "configuration", state is for "what changed". function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c+1)}>{count}</button>; }
props-state-intro.q: What is the difference between props and state in React?
props-state-intro.qsub: What does it mean that props are immutable? What happens if you try to modify props directly?
props-state-intro.what:
Definition: There are two types of data in React:

  • Props — come from outside (like function arguments). Read-only.
  • State — lives inside a component, created with useState. It can change, and when it changes the UI updates.

One-line rule: If it changes, it belongs in state; if it doesn’t change, it belongs in props.
props-state-intro.analogy: Props = your birth name — given by your parents, you can’t change it yourself. State = your mood — it’s yours, it changes constantly, and when it changes your expression changes too.
props-state-intro.why: This split creates a "one-way data flow" — data always moves from top to bottom. So when the UI looks wrong you can go up the tree to find the source. If a child could change its parent’s data, tracing would become impossible.
pros: Data flows in a single direction — debugging is easy
Components that use only props are pure — same props produce the same output
Keeping state in one place gives a "single source of truth"
cons: In a deep tree, props may need to be passed down five levels (prop drilling)
Beginners find it difficult to decide which data should be state
gotchas: Never mutate props — they are read-only, otherwise bugs stay silent
Don’t create state for values that can be derived from props (total = price × qty should not be state)
setState does not change the value immediately — the new value is available on the next render

props.name: Props & Immutability
props.desc: Props are read-only inputs flowing parent → child. Mutating props directly breaks the one-way data flow contract.
props.q: Why are props immutable? What happens to child components when a parent re-renders?
props.qsub: What is prop drilling and what are the solutions? When is prop drilling actually fine?
props.what: Definition: Props are the data given from parent to child. React treats them as read-only — a child cannot change props. React's rule: "every component should behave like a pure function with respect to its props".
props.why: Immutability is necessary because React reference compares (Object.is). If you modify an object internally, the reference remains the same, React will think nothing changed, and the UI will not update. Therefore always create a new object/array.

Reference comparison lets React perform fast diffs
Composition with children becomes very flexible

Spread chains become long for deep nested updates
Prop drilling causes pain in deep trees

Write your own props before spreading, otherwise the user cannot override them

class-vs-functional.name: Class vs Functional Components
class-vs-functional.desc: Class components use lifecycle methods and this; functional components use hooks. Hooks give functions all the same capabilities — and more.
class-vs-functional.q: What are the key differences between class and functional components? Why did the React team move to hooks?
class-vs-functional.qsub: What does a class component have that functional components still cannot fully replicate?
class-vs-functional.what:
Definition: In React, components were written in two ways. Class (before 2019) had this.state, this.setState, and lifecycle methods. Functional (today) uses hooks for the same things, without this.

New code today is always functional. Class appears only in legacy code and Error Boundaries.
class-vs-functional.why: In a class, the logic for a single task was split across three lifecycle methods (subscribe componentDidMount, update componentDidUpdate, cleanup componentWillUnmount). In hooks, all three are in a single useEffect. And the "wrapper hell" of HOC/render-props for logic reuse is now eliminated by custom hooks.

Logic reuse is easy with custom hooks
Related logic in one place, not scattered across lifecycle methods
cons: Hooks have their own rules (top level only)
Stale closures introduce a new class-like bug pattern
Class is still required for Error Boundaries
gotchas: Error Boundaries can only be created with classes — this is a favorite interview question
In classes, this.setState merged state; useState replaces it
A functional component re-executes the entire function on every render — variables are recreated

state-basics.name: State & Re-renders
state-basics.desc: State is private, mutable data that when changed schedules a re-render. React batches state updates for efficiency.
state-basics.q: What triggers a re-render in React? What does NOT trigger a re-render?
state-basics.qsub: If you call setState with the same value as current state, does React re-render?
state-basics.what:
Definition: State is a component's private data that persists across re-renders and causes React to re-render when it changes. const [x, setX] = useState(initial).

Two important truths: (1) setX does not change the value immediately — the new value appears on the next render; (2) React batches all setState calls from an event into a single re-render.
state-basics.analogy: Photo. Each render is a photo that captures the values at that moment. setX queues a new photo — but you still have the old photo in hand.
state-basics.why: Without understanding this, the most classic bug appears — writing setCount(count+1) three times results in +1, not +3. Because each time count comes from the same old snapshot. With a functional update setCount(c => c+1), React provides the latest value, so you get +3.
pros: Batching makes one event = one render, good performance
Functional update prevents race conditions
Lazy init ensures expensive initial calculation runs only once
cons: The asynchronous nature confuses beginners a lot
Object/array state must be manually copied
When many related useState hooks exist, useReducer is better
gotchas: Reading the value immediately after setState gives the OLD value — this is not a bug, it's by design
Anything that depends on the old value should always use a functional update
useState(expensiveFn()) runs on every render — write useState(() => expensiveFn())

vdom.name: Virtual DOM
vdom.desc: An in-memory JS object tree mirroring the real DOM — React diffs the new vs old tree and only applies minimal real DOM changes.
vdom.q: What is the Virtual DOM and why does React use it? Does it always make things faster?
vdom.qsub: What is the actual cost of the Virtual DOM? When would direct DOM manipulation be faster?
vdom.what: Definition: Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the real DOM. When state changes, React creates a new virtual tree, compares it with the old one, and applies only what changed to the real DOM.
vdom.analogy: House blueprint. Before tearing down a wall, you make a blueprint, compare it with the old blueprint, and only tear down the wall that truly needs to change. You don’t collapse the whole house.
vdom.why:
DOM operations are expensive — each change can trigger layout/paint. If React rebuilt the entire DOM on every state change, the app would stall. Diffing happens on JavaScript objects (cheap), and only minimal updates go to the DOM (expensive but few).

But the truth is — the Virtual DOM is not faster than manually optimized DOM code. It is "quite fast" while allowing you to write declaratively. Speed isn’t the main point; developer experience (DX) is.
pros: You can write declaratively, and React handles the optimization.
Diffing happens in JavaScript — DOM operations are minimal.
Cross-platform — the same concept works in React Native as well
cons: Extra memory — two trees need to be kept.
Slower than manually optimized vanilla JavaScript.
Svelte/SolidJS remove this layer and are faster.
gotchas: The Virtual DOM isn’t for “fast” — it enables declarative coding.
If an element’s type changes, React does not reuse the node — the entire subtree’s state is lost.
React 19 still uses a VDOM — Fiber is its implementation, not a replacement.

keys.name: Keys in Lists
keys.desc: Keys help React identify which items in a list changed, were added, or removed — critical for correct reconciliation.
keys.q: Why does React need keys? What happens if you use index as a key? When is index as key actually safe?
keys.qsub: What is key remounting? When would you deliberately change a key to reset a component?
keys.what: Definition: A key is a special prop that tells React which item is the same item between two renders of a list. Without a key, React matches by position, which becomes incorrect when items are added, removed, or reordered.
keys.analogy: Roll number in a class. If you identify a student by position (first, second) and a student leaves from the middle, everyone's identification shifts. A roll number (key) prevents that.
keys.why: This is not just about hiding a warning — it's a real bug. If you add an item in the middle of a list using an index key: React sees a new item at position 0, assumes "it's the same old item with changed text", and reuses the DOM node. Result — typed text in an input ends up in the wrong row, a checkbox stays ticked on the wrong item.

On reorder, React moves nodes instead of recreating them
Changing a key to reset is a clean trick

A Math.random() key remounts on every render — very slow

You cannot read the key from props — props.key is undefined, React keeps it internally

work-loop.name: Work Loop & Time Slicing
work-loop.desc: The Fiber work loop processes one Fiber node at a time, yielding back to the browser every ~5ms so frames aren't blocked — enabling interruptible rendering.
work-loop.q: What is time slicing in React? How does the work loop enable rendering without blocking the browser?
work-loop.qsub: What API does React use to yield back to the browser (MessageChannel, requestIdleCallback, etc.) and why?
work-loop.what: Definition: The work loop is React's main engine. It is a while loop that processes one fiber at a time, and after each fiber asks — "has my 5ms time expired?" If yes, it yields (lets the browser run) and resumes from the same point in the next frame.
work-loop.analogy: Studying with a break every 25 minutes (Pomodoro). The work gets completed, but you don’t become a machine — essential things happen in between.
work-loop.why: The browser creates a frame in 16.6 ms (60 fps). If React holds the thread for 200 ms, 12 frames will be dropped — the user will think the app has hung. With 5 ms slices, React keeps working while the browser can also paint. The total work time remains the same, but the app feels responsive.
pros: The main thread is never blocked for long periods
User input is always responsive
Low-priority work can be interrupted or discarded
cons: The total work increases slightly (scheduling overhead)
Available only in concurrent roots
In synchronous updates this loop does not yield
gotchas: Time slicing does not make your code faster — it only splits it
A component’s render does not pause in the middle — it pauses after the fiber, so a heavy component can still block
In synchronous updates (e.g., click) the work loop does not yield

batching.name: Batching (React 17 vs React 18)
batching.desc: React 17 only batches state updates inside React event handlers. React 18 batches ALL updates — including setTimeout, promises, and native events — automatically.
batching.q: What is state batching? How does React 18's automatic batching differ from React 17? How do you opt out?
batching.qsub: What is flushSync and when would you need it?
batching.what:
Definition: Batching means combining all setState calls that occur in the same tick into a single re-render.

In React 17 batching happened only inside React event handlers. Inside setTimeout, promises, or native listeners each setState triggered a separate render. In React 18 batching occurs everywhere — this is called “automatic batching”.
batching.why: Three setState calls = three renders, meaning three full tree diffs and three DOM commits. Batching reduces it to one render. In React 17 the code fetch().then(() => { setLoading(false); setData(d); }) caused two renders — there was a frame where loading was false but data had not arrived yet (flash of empty state). In React 18 this bug disappears automatically.
pros: Fewer renders = better performance
Inconsistent UI state never appears
You get it in React 18 without any extra work
cons: flushSync hurts performance — use only when necessary
Upgrading from React 17 can change some code behavior
Code that reads the DOM immediately after setState breaks
gotchas: A new batch starts after an await — the previous batch ends
flushSync should be used only for DOM measurements or scrolling — otherwise avoid it
Even with batching, the state variable remains its old value immediately after setState

React 18 feature — batching everywhere, not just in event handlers

render-commit.name: Render Phase vs Commit Phase
render-commit.desc: Render phase: pure, interruptible work — React builds the new Fiber tree. Commit phase: synchronous, non-interruptible — React applies DOM mutations and runs effects.
render-commit.q: What is the difference between the render phase and commit phase? Why must the render phase be pure?
render-commit.qsub: In which phase do useEffect and useLayoutEffect run? Why does useLayoutEffect need to be synchronous?
render-commit.what:
Definition: Every update occurs in two phases:

  • Render (thinking) — component functions run, a new tree is created, diffing happens. No DOM changes. It can pause, rerun, or be cancelled.
  • Commit (work) — DOM updates, refs are set, effects run. This happens all at once, without pausing.
render-commit.analogy: Drawing the house blueprint (render) vs building the wall (commit). You can tear up and redraw the blueprint ten times — no loss. Once the wall is built you cannot stop it midway.
render-commit.why:
This split explains everything:

  • Do not perform side effects in the render phase — because they may run twice or be cancelled (StrictMode double-invokes for this reason).
  • useEffect runs after the commit (after the browser paint) — therefore it feels asynchronous.
  • useLayoutEffect runs inside the commit, before the paint — making it suitable for DOM measurements but it is blocking.
pros: Render being interruptible keeps the UI responsive
Commit is atomic — the user never sees a half-finished UI
Effect timing is predictable
cons: The purity rule of the render phase is easy to break
Beginners forget the difference between the two effect hooks
If the commit is long, it will still block
gotchas: Do not read/write the DOM, fetch, or set timers in the render phase
useLayoutEffect is blocking — use it only when you need to measure the DOM before paint
Refs are set during commit, so ref.current can be null during render
terms: React is figuring out what changed — pure, interruptible
React is actually changing the DOM — synchronous, uninterruptible

scheduler.name: React Scheduler & Priority Lanes
scheduler.desc: React's scheduler assigns priority lanes to updates (SyncLane, InputContinuousLane, DefaultLane, IdleLane) and processes high-priority work first.
scheduler.q: How does React prioritize which updates to process first? What are lanes in React?
scheduler.qsub: How does startTransition use the scheduler to deprioritize an update?
scheduler.what:
Definition: The Scheduler is React's priority system. Every update gets a lane. More urgent lanes are processed first; less urgent work waits.

Priority order (topmost most urgent): Sync (discrete events like click/input) → InputContinuous (hover, drag) → Default (normal setState) → Transition (startTransition) → Idle (offscreen).
scheduler.analogy: Hospital emergency ward. A heart attack (click) is handled first, a fracture (hover) next, a routine checkup (transition) waits. But even routine cases eventually get a number (prevents starvation).
scheduler.why: Without priority all work is equal — filtering a large list would block typing. Lanes allow React to say "typing first, filtered list later", and interrupt the filter work to show typing. useTransition does exactly this.

Priority check via bitmask is almost free
Built-in protection against starvation

Giving the wrong priority can make the UI feel laggy

Code after async/await inside startTransition does NOT run in the transition

fiber-arch.name: React Fiber Architecture
fiber-arch.desc: The complete rewrite of React's reconciler (React 16+). Fiber turns the render tree into a linked list of units of work that can be paused, aborted, and resumed.
fiber-arch.q: What is React Fiber and why was it a complete rewrite? What problem does it solve over the old stack reconciler?
fiber-arch.qsub: What is a Fiber node? What properties does it hold?
fiber-arch.what:
Definition: Fiber is the reconciliation engine in React 16+. For each component, a fiber node is created — a plain object that contains the component's type, props, state, and pointers to its parent, child, and sibling.

This turns recursion into a linked-list traversal, and you can pause the linked list in the middle. That's the whole point of Fiber.
fiber-arch.analogy: Reading a book. Recursion = reading the entire book in one breath; if someone stops you, you have to start over. Fiber = placing a bookmark — you continue from where you stopped.
fiber-arch.why:
In React 15, reconciliation was recursive. Recursion uses the JavaScript call stack and the call stack cannot be paused in the middle. A tree of 5,000 components blocks the main thread for up to 200 ms, freezing the user's typing.

With Fiber, React can ask after each node, "Does the browser have any urgent work?" If yes, it pauses, lets the browser run, then resumes from that point. This is why useTransition, Suspense, and concurrent rendering became possible.
pros: Rendering can be paused — UI does not freeze
Priority system possible — urgent updates run first
A single update can be dropped or restarted
cons: It is quite complex under the hood
Render function may run twice — breaks impure code
Debugging becomes difficult
gotchas: Fiber is not a replacement for the Virtual DOM — it is a way to implement the VDOM
Render phase is interruptible, commit phase is NOT — commit always completes in one go

reconciliation.name: Reconciliation & Diffing Algorithm
reconciliation.desc: React's O(n) algorithm for comparing two trees using two heuristics: elements of different types produce different trees; keys identify stable elements across renders.
reconciliation.q: Explain how React's diffing algorithm works. What are its two key assumptions that make it O(n) instead of O(n³)?
reconciliation.qsub:
What happens in the diff when a parent changes from a
to a ? What about when you reorder list items with vs without keys?
reconciliation.what:
Definition: Reconciliation is the algorithm that compares the old fiber tree with the new element tree. A perfect tree-diff is O(n³) — for 1,000 nodes it would require a trillion operations. React applies two heuristics to make it O(n):

  1. Different type = different tree. Do not compare; discard the old one and create a new one.
  2. Match items on the same level using their key.
reconciliation.why:
These two rules are practically always true — developers do not expect the same content when changing a <div> to a <span>. As a result, React becomes 1,000× faster.

But there is a major side effect: changing the type discards the entire state of the subtree. This is the real cause of the “my input reset” bug.

DOM node reuse on same type — state is preserved
Efficient list reordering with keys

If the type changes, the subtree's state silently disappears
The same component cannot be moved to two different locations
gotchas: Never define a component inside another component — it remounts on every render
90% of “input reset” issues are caused by this — the type or key changed
React treats the same position + same type as the SAME component, even if logically different

controlled-uncontrolled.name: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components

strictmode.name: StrictMode
strictmode.desc: A development-only tool that double-invokes render/lifecycle functions to surface side effect bugs and deprecated API usage.
strictmode.q: What does StrictMode do? Why does it call some functions twice in development?
strictmode.qsub: If StrictMode causes bugs by double-invoking effects, what does that reveal about your code?
strictmode.what:
Definition: <StrictMode> is a development-only wrapper. It doesn’t render anything — it just tells React to "check extra strictly". The most visible effect: components render twice and effects run twice (mount → unmount → mount).

In a production build it does absolutely nothing.
strictmode.analogy: Fire drill. There’s no fire, but the alarm is deliberately sounded to see if the evacuation route actually works.
strictmode.why:
In React 18+, future features (Offscreen, preserving state with Suspense) may unmount a component and mount it again. If your effect cleanup is wrong — timer not cleared, subscription not unsubscribed — it will crash later. StrictMode reveals that bug today.

Seeing an API call run twice is not a bug — it’s StrictMode. To “fix” it, don’t add a ref guard; the real fix is to abort in the cleanup.
pros: Catches missing cleanup and impure renders immediately
Zero cost in production
Warns about deprecated APIs
cons: Beginners get confused seeing logs/network twice
Some older libraries break in StrictMode
Console noise increases
gotchas: Running twice is DEV-ONLY — in production it runs once
Don’t remove StrictMode to “fix” — it’s hiding a bug, not fixing it
Render functions should be pure — no mutations or side effects

element-component-instance.name: React Element vs Component vs Instance
element-component-instance.desc: Element: a plain object describing what to render. Component: a function/class that returns elements. Instance: only class components have instances (this).
element-component-instance.q: What is the difference between a React element, a React component, and a React instance?
element-component-instance.qsub: Why don't functional components have instances? What does that mean for refs?
element-component-instance.what:
Definition: Three different things that people mix up:

  • Component = recipe (function Card)
  • Element = order slip (<Card title="Hi"/> — an object, nothing has run yet)
  • Instance = actual dish (fiber node that holds state, effects, DOM pointer)
element-component-instance.analogy: Recipe (component) → order slip (element) → plated dish (instance). One recipe can produce 100 order slips, each order slip creates a separate dish.
element-component-instance.why:
Understanding this distinction clears up two common questions:

  • "Does creating an element run the component?" No. <Card/> only creates an object. React decides when to call Card().
  • "Where does state live?" Not in the component (it’s just a function), not in the element (it’s immutable) — it lives in the instance/fiber. Therefore when the fiber is destroyed, the state disappears.

State is managed by React through the instance, not by you
Unlimited independent instances from the same component

You cannot directly access the instance (in functional components)

rules-of-hooks.name: Rules of Hooks & Their Internals
rules-of-hooks.desc: Hooks must be called at top level and only from React functions. React stores hook state in a linked list on the Fiber node, indexed by call order.
rules-of-hooks.q: Why can't hooks be called inside conditionals or loops? What would break internally if you did?
rules-of-hooks.qsub: How does React know which useState call corresponds to which state value across re-renders?
rules-of-hooks.what:
Definition: Two rules:

  1. Call hooks only at the top level — not inside if, loop, or nested functions.
  2. Call them only inside a React function component or custom hook.

Reason in one line: React identifies hooks by order, not name.
rules-of-hooks.analogy: People standing in a line without names. Counting tells you who is who — "first, second, third". If the second person sometimes skips the line, the third will mistakenly become the second.
rules-of-hooks.why: Inside a fiber, hooks are stored in a linked list. On each render React walks the list from the start — first useState call → first node, second call → second node. If you place a hook inside an if and the condition becomes false, the whole list shifts — the state for name would be taken by age. React cannot detect this, which is why the lint rule exists.
pros: Order-based lookup is very fast — no key/name needed
Hooks can be composed because the order is predictable
Lint rule catches 99% of mistakes

"Rendered fewer hooks than expected" error can be confusing
All hooks must be written before any early return
gotchas: Install eslint-plugin-react-hooks — it enforces the rule automatically
Don’t put hooks inside try/catch — it’s also a conditional path

usememo.name: useMemo — When to Use & When Not To
usememo.desc: Memoizes the result of an expensive computation. Only recalculates when dependencies change. Costs memory and code complexity — only worth it for genuinely expensive work.
usememo.q: When should you use useMemo? What is the overhead of useMemo itself? When does it hurt performance?
usememo.qsub: Prove that useMemo is not a semantic guarantee — React can choose to discard memoized values. Does that matter?
usememo.what:
Definition: useMemo(fn, deps) remembers the result of a calculation. If dependencies do not change, fn does not run again — the previous result is returned.

Two valid reasons: (1) truly expensive calculation, (2) keep reference stable so that downstream memo/effect does not break.
usememo.why:
The other reason is more important. const opts = {a:1} creates a new object on every render. If that object is passed as a prop to a React.memo child, memoization becomes useless — the child re-renders each time. useMemo keeps the reference stable.

But don’t memoize everything. useMemo has its own cost — dependency comparison, memory. Memoizing a simple a+b is wasteful. React 19’s compiler is starting to handle this automatically.

Reference stability preserves downstream memo chains
Prevents infinite loops in effects
cons: It has its own cost — memory + dependency comparison
Incorrect deps cause silent stale value bugs
Code becomes harder to read
gotchas: Measure with the Profiler first, then memoize — don’t guess
useMemo is not a guarantee — React may discard the cache under memory pressure
Memoization only helps when a new object/array is passed as a prop on every render

usecallback.name: useCallback — Referential Stability
usecallback.desc: Returns a memoized function reference that only changes when dependencies change. Critical when passing callbacks to memoized child components.
usecallback.q: Why does useCallback exist? When does it actually help performance vs when is it wasted?
usecallback.qsub: If useCallback is just useMemo returning a function, when would you choose one over the other?
usecallback.what:
Definition: useCallback(fn, deps) = useMemo(() => fn, deps). It remembers the function so that the same reference is obtained on every render.

In JavaScript, every render creates a new function object for () => {} — it looks the same but the reference is different. Because of this, a child using React.memo breaks.
usecallback.why:
useCallback alone is useless. Its benefit appears only when the receiver cares about the reference — i.e., the child is wrapped in React.memo, or the function is a dependency of an effect, or it is passed into a custom hook.

If the child is not memoized, adding useCallback only adds cost with zero benefit.

Prevents infinite loops in effects
Predictable for custom hook consumers

Largest source of stale closures
Applying to every handler makes code heavy

usereducer.name: useReducer — Complex State Logic
usereducer.desc: An alternative to useState for complex state transitions. Takes (state, action) => newState. Makes state logic testable and colocated.

Definition: useReducer(reducer, initial) — when several state values are related, keep them in a single reducer instead of separate useState calls. Every change is an "action".

usecontext.name: useContext — Performance Trap
usecontext.desc: Subscribes a component to the nearest context value. Every context value change re-renders ALL consumers — even if they only use part of the value.
usecontext.q: What is the performance problem with useContext? How do you prevent unnecessary re-renders from context changes?
usecontext.qsub: What are the patterns to split context to avoid over-rendering? How does Zustand solve this differently?
usecontext.what:
Definition: Context is a way to avoid prop drilling. A Provider supplies a value, and anywhere in the tree you can retrieve that value with useContext.

Performance trap: When the context value changes, all consumers re-render — even if they only used a small part of that value.
usecontext.analogy: Home WiFi. You don’t need to run cables to every room (prop drilling). But if you change the WiFi password, all devices disconnect — even if one only needed the printer.

The most common bug: <Ctx.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>. This object is new on every render, so all consumers re-render on each parent render — even if the user hasn’t changed. Fix: memoize the value with useMemo.

Another fix: split the context — put mutable data in a separate context and keep unchanged data (functions) in another. Then components that only use the functions won’t re-render when the data changes.

usestate.name: useState Internals

usestate.what:
Definition: useState creates a node in the memoizedState linked list on the fiber. That node holds — the current value, and an update queue that contains pending setState calls.

  • Why setting the same value does not trigger a render — React compares with Object.is and bails out. However, the first render may still happen (React checks once).

useeffect.name: useEffect — Timing, Deps, Cleanup
useeffect.desc: Runs after paint, asynchronously. The dependency array controls when it re-runs. The cleanup function runs before the next effect or on unmount.
useeffect.q: Explain useEffect's full lifecycle: when does it run, when does cleanup run, what is the dependency array contract?
useeffect.qsub: What happens if you put a function in the dependency array? How do you fix the infinite loop?
useeffect.what:
Definition: useEffect(fn, deps) tells React "after commit + paint do this work". The deps array indicates when to run again.

  • No array → every render
  • [] → only on mount (and twice in StrictMode development)
  • [a, b] → when a or b change

Cleanup runs every time before the effect runs again — not only on unmount.
useeffect.analogy: Turning off the light when leaving a room. You turn it off every time you leave — not just when you move out of the house.
useeffect.why:
Cleanup running every time is exactly what saves you from a race condition. You change the user quickly — 3 fetches start. Without cleanup, whichever arrives latest wins, even if it is for the old user. With an abort in cleanup, only the latest request survives.

React 18's guidance: useEffect is not ideal for data fetching. Use React Query or a framework loader — they handle caching, dedup, retry, everything.

Deps provide automatic re-sync
Easily wrapped in custom hooks
cons: Wrong tool for data fetching — leads to waterfall and race conditions
Incorrect deps cause infinite loops or stale data
Object/function deps change on every render

Do not use object/function as deps — extract primitives or use useMemo/useCallback
Do not silence the eslint exhaustive-deps warning — understand it, it is often correct

uselayouteffect.name: useLayoutEffect vs useEffect
uselayouteffect.desc: useLayoutEffect fires synchronously after DOM mutations but before paint — identical to componentDidMount/Update. useEffect fires after paint.
uselayouteffect.q: When would you use useLayoutEffect over useEffect? Give a concrete real-world example.
uselayouteffect.qsub: Why does React warn against useLayoutEffect in SSR? How do you work around it?
uselayouteffect.what:
Definition: Both run after commit, but timing differs:

  • useLayoutEffect — after DOM update, BEFORE paint. Synchronous, blocks the browser.
  • useEffect — AFTER paint. Asynchronous, does not block the browser.

Default is always useEffect. useLayoutEffect only when you need to measure the DOM and change it within the same frame.
uselayouteffect.analogy: Fixing hair before taking a photo (useLayoutEffect) vs fixing it after the photo is taken (useEffect). In the latter case, the first photo will show bad hair.
uselayouteffect.why: Classic tooltip case: on the initial render the tooltip is at (0,0). If you set the position with useEffect, the user sees the tooltip in the corner for one frame then it jumps — flicker. With useLayoutEffect the position is set before paint, so the user never sees it in the wrong place.

DOM measurement is guaranteed to be accurate
Stays in sync with layout

Does not run in SSR, gives a warning
Overuse degrades performance

In SSR useLayoutEffect gives a warning — create an isomorphic wrapper
Do not perform heavy calculations inside it; it will block the entire paint

useref.name: useRef — Beyond DOM Access
useref.desc: useRef returns a stable object { current } that persists across renders without triggering re-renders. Use it for: DOM access, timers, previous values, and mutable instance variables.

useref.what:
Definition: useRef(init) gives an object { current: init } that stays the same object for the component's entire life. Changing .current does not cause a re-render.

useref.analogy: Pocket. You can put anything in it, take it out — no one needs to be notified (no re-render). State is a notice board — when something changes, everyone sees it.
useref.why: Sometimes you need to remember a value but the UI does not depend on it — interval id, a "is first render" flag, previous props. If you store it in state, every change would cause an unnecessary render. Ref fills exactly this gap.

zustand.q: How does Zustand work under the hood? How does it avoid the re-render problem that Context has?
zustand.qsub: Compare Zustand, Context+useReducer, and Redux for a mid-size app. What are the tradeoffs?
zustand.what:
Definition: Zustand is a tiny (~1KB) state library. You create a store with create(), and it becomes a hook. No Provider, no boilerplate.

The biggest difference from Context: selector support. You can subscribe to only one field of the store — changes to anything else will not cause your component to render.

Definition: In atomic state (Jotai, Recoil) there is no single large store — there are many small atoms. Each component subscribes only to the atoms it uses.

atomic-state.analogy: Excel. Each cell is an atom. =A1+B1 is a derived cell. When A1 changes, only the formula that depends on A1 runs — the whole sheet is not recalculated.
atomic-state.why: In Zustand/Redux you have to write selectors to avoid extra renders. In the atomic model the subscription is automatically precise — you use an atom, and you subscribe only to it. redux.q: Explain the full Redux data flow. What is the role of middleware? When is Redux overkill?
redux.qsub: What is the difference between Redux Thunk and Redux Saga? What problem does each solve?
redux.what:
Definition: Redux is a predictable state container. Three rules: (1) single store, (2) state is read-only — you can only change it by dispatching actions, (3) changes happen via pure reducers.

Data flows in one direction: dispatch(action) → middleware → reducer → naya state → UI.
redux.analogy: Court’s record room. No file can be changed directly. You submit an application (action), the clerk (reducer) follows the rules to create a new record, and the old record remains traceable.
redux.why:
The real benefit of Redux is traceability — DevTools shows every action, every state change, enabling time-travel debugging. In large teams with complex apps, you can answer “who changed this state?” in five seconds.

But in 2026, don’t write plain Redux — use Redux Toolkit. And don’t use Redux for server data; use React Query instead.

Predictable — same actions produce same state
Middleware enables cross-cutting logic (logging, analytics, persistence)

Wrong tool for server data
Overkill for small/medium apps

rerender-causes.desc: A component re-renders when: its state changes, its parent re-renders, context it consumes changes, or its key changes. Props being the same is NOT enough to prevent re-renders.
rerender-causes.q: List every cause of a React re-render. What is the most common source of unnecessary re-renders in production apps?
rerender-causes.qsub: If a parent re-renders but passes the same props to a child, does the child re-render? What stops it?
rerender-causes.what:
Definition: A component re-renders for only four reasons:

  1. Its own state changed
  2. Its parent re-rendered
  3. A context value it consumes changed
  4. Its hook (useSyncExternalStore etc.) sent an update

Changing props is not in the list — props change only when the parent renders, so the actual reason is #2.
rerender-causes.why: The biggest misconception: "props changed, that's why it rendered". The truth is the opposite — the child rendered because the parent rendered, even if the props are exactly the same. Understanding this shows the right path to optimization: before memoizing props, stopping the parent's render or pushing state down is more effective.

Pushing state down is the cleanest fix
Composition is better and cheaper than memo

Not every render is slow — measure first

"If props are the same, there will be no render" — WRONG. It will happen without memo.
Push state down first; memo is the last option

memo-usememo-usecallback.what:
Definition: They are three separate things but work together:

  • React.memo — component render is prevented
  • useMemo — value reference is kept stable
  • useCallback — function reference is kept stable

Rule: Without React.memo, the other two are useless (except for effect dependencies).
memo-usememo-usecallback.analogy: Lock and key. React.memo is the lock. useMemo/useCallback keep the key the same. If there is no lock, the key is meaningless — the door stays open.
memo-usememo-usecallback.why: If any link in the chain breaks, the whole effort is wasted. Therefore the correct way to memoize is: first measure with the Profiler, then build the entire chain, then measure again to see if it really made a difference. A memo added by guesswork is often just cost.

Clear impact on list performance
Effect loops stop

If the chain breaks in one place, the whole effort is wasted
Applying it everywhere is often a net negative

concurrent-mode.what:
Definition: Concurrent React means that React can pause, resume, or discard a render. This is not a feature you turn "on" — it is a capability provided by createRoot, and you use it with useTransition/useDeferredValue/Suspense.

concurrent-mode.why: In older React, once a render started it had to finish completely. While rendering a heavy list, your typing would freeze. In concurrent mode, React says "typing is more important" — it discards half of the list render, shows the typing, then resumes the list.

Suspense and streaming SSR are built on this

suspense.qsub: What is the "fetch-then-render" vs "render-as-you-fetch" pattern? How does Suspense enable the latter?
suspense.what:
Definition: <Suspense fallback={...}> is a boundary. If any component inside it is "not ready yet" (lazy chunk loading, or data arriving), React shows the fallback and once ready, the actual content.

This moves the loading state from inside the component to the tree structure.
suspense.analogy: Leaving an empty plate at a restaurant. The plate (fallback) stays until the food arrives — the table doesn’t look empty. When the food arrives, the plate is removed.
suspense.why:
Without Suspense, each component had to write if (loading) return <Spinner/> — 10 components = 10 separate spinners, and the page would flicker. With Suspense you decide in one place what the loading UI for the whole section will be.

Important: a plain useEffect fetch does not trigger Suspense. Suspense requires a Suspense-enabled source — React Query (suspense mode), RSC, framework loader, or use().

If a component has import { api } from './api', it's hard to replace it in tests — you have to mock the module. With a Provider, you can simply attach a fake provider in the test, and the component won't even notice.

rtl-philosophy.desc: "Test the behaviour users see, not implementation details." Queries mirror what users and assistive technology perceive — avoiding brittle tests tied to component internals.
rtl-philosophy.q: What is the React Testing Library philosophy? Why is testing implementation details harmful?
rtl-philosophy.qsub: What is the difference between getBy, queryBy, and findBy? When do you use each?
rtl-philosophy.what:
Definition: RTL has a single principle — "the more the tests resemble user usage, the more confidence they give". Therefore RTL does not touch state, props, or internal functions. It only interacts with what is visible on the screen.

Query priority: getByRole > getByLabelText > getByText > ... > getByTestId (the last resort).
rtl-philosophy.analogy: Car test drive. You don’t count pistons by opening the engine — you drive it to see if it runs, stalls, or stops. If you replace the engine and it still runs, the test should pass.
rtl-philosophy.why:
If you test implementation details, the tests will break on every refactor — even if the app is working perfectly. Those tests block you instead of helping. RTL tests survive refactors and only fail when something truly breaks.

Bonus: Using getByRole automatically tests accessibility — if a button lacks an accessible name, the query will fail.

what-to-test.what:
Definition: Testing everything is wasteful. Test only where the damage from breaking is high:

  1. User flows — login, checkout, form submit
  2. Business logic — price calculation, permission, validation
  3. Edge cases — empty, error, loading, very long text

Traditional pyramid (many unit tests) is a poor fit for React because React bugs often occur between components, not inside them. Therefore the "trophy" model — integration tests provide the most value: a test that fills a form, submits it, and checks the result, gives more confidence than 10 unit tests.

Don’t chase 100% coverage — it only shows that code ran, not that it ran correctly.

nextjs-overview.what:

nextjs-hydration.what:
Definition: The server sends HTML (it renders but is not interactive). Then JavaScript arrives and React attaches its tree to that HTML — adding event handlers. This is called hydration.

The fix pattern is simple: keep the first render identical to the server, and show browser-specific things inside useEffect (i.e., on the second render).

And by writing the schema with zod in one place you get both type and validation.

error-boundaries-eco.what:
Definition: A raw class boundary only catches errors — it provides no way to reset. In practice you need: a retry button, automatic reset when the route changes, and error logging.

react-error-boundary library provides all of this — onReset, resetKeys, and the useErrorBoundary hook (to forward async errors to the boundary).
error-boundaries-eco.why: Async errors are the biggest gap. If fetch fails, the boundary does not catch it — you have to keep it in state and render it yourself. With useErrorBoundary().showBoundary(err) you can send that error to the boundary, so error handling stays in one place.

prop-types-defaults.what:
Definition: Three legacy things that appear in interviews:

  • PropTypes — runtime type check. Useless today compared to TypeScript. Removed in React 19.
  • defaultProps — deprecated for function components. Now use JS default parameters.
  • Callback ref — still useful, and React 19 also supports a cleanup function.
prop-types-defaults.why: It is important to know because (a) you will find it in legacy codebases, (b) interviewers ask "PropTypes vs TypeScript", and (c) callback ref is still a real tool when you need to do something on a node's mount/unmount — this does not happen with useRef because changing a ref provides no notification.

nextjs-optimisations.what:
Definition: Next.js's built-in optimizers:

  • next/image — automatic resize, WebP/AVIF, lazy load, blur placeholder
  • next/font — fonts self-hosted at build time, zero layout shift
  • metadata export — SEO tags on the server
  • next/script — control over loading of third-party scripts
nextjs-optimisations.why: These three directly affect Core Web Vitals (which count in Google ranking). An image without width/height gives CLS; if Google Fonts come from the CDN there's an extra DNS + connection + FOUT; if metadata is set on the client the crawler doesn't see it at all.
